newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bomb kills 21 on train in Algeria's week of death.
newsitem.headline: Bomb kills 21 on train in Algeria's week of death.

text.p: A bomb, believed planted by Moslem rebels, killed at least 21 train passengers and wounded 20 near Algiers on Friday, Algerian security forces said.

It sealed a week of violence in which more than 150 people have died. Most had their throats cut in attacks linked by some diplomats to fundamentalist attempts to disrupt a parliamentary election due on June 5.
The security forces said the home-made bomb went off at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) under a passenger train near Oued El Kerma station in the Algiers suburb of Gue de Constantine.
"This explosion, according to a preliminary count, caused the death of 21 people, and wounded 20 others," the forces said in a statement carried on Algeria's official news agency APS.
It gave few other details but termed the bomb a "criminal act", Algerian official language for attacks by Moslem rebels who have been fighting to overthrow the authorities for more than five years.

Some diplomats have linked the latest surge of violence to the advance towards Algeria's first parliamentary elections in more than five years. Well over 300 people have died in the few weeks since the election date of June 5 was announced.
Voters among Algeria's 29 million people are to elect an assembly whose dissolution by the authorities in January 1992 led Moslem fundamentalists, who had headed that poll, to take up arms.
Friday's bomb destroyed the second coach of the passenger train, normally packed but only lightly loaded on the Algerian Moslem weekend, an eyewitness told Reuters by telephone.
"The bomb made a seven-metre (yard) large crater...The traffic was suspended on the train line between Khemiss Meliana and Algiers," a resident of Oued El Kerma said.
Khemiss Meliana is located at 100 km (60 miles) south of Algiers.
The attack was a harsh reminder of rebels' ability to use bombs and strike in the crowded capital, Algiers, home to around three million people.
Car bombs brought mass carnage earlier this year but had recently been eclipsed by the horror of night raids on isolated villages and the merciless slaughter of their inhabitants.
In two raids this week at least 135 people, including babies, girls, and old people, were killed -- most with their throats cut.

In the first massacre, in the farming community of Baouch Boughlef-Khemisti only 25 km (15 miles) south of Algiers, 93 people were hacked to death, the highest death toll in a single raid in the more than five years of violence.
The authorities described the raid as one of "unprecedented savagery" and the handful of survivors told of seeing the throats of their loved ones slit and their heads cut off.

The second raid only 24 hours later was on Omaria village, about 50 km (30 miles) south of the capital. Algerian newspapers said 42 people were killed in the massacre which went into the early hours of Wednesday.
About 60,000 people have died since the violence erupted in 1992, and President Liamine Zeroual sees the June election as a major step towards pulling the country out of crisis.
